newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers' strike -- sectors hit.
newsitem.headline: French truckers' strike -- sectors hit.

text.p: A nine-day-old French truckers' strike has taken a heavy toll on France's fuel and farm industries and threatens hundreds of businesses and factories cut off from markets and suppliers, officials said on Tuesday.

Refineries and fuel depots were among the primary targets of the truckers, who have erected nearly 180 roadblocks to push for higher wages, shorter working hours and earlier retirement. On Monday they started to close in on the capital.
Truckers' unions and employers said they made little progress in a fifth round of talks on Tuesday.
Fuel shortages and rationing were reported in many regions, fishermen pulled up their lines as perishable goods rotted on clogged roads, and food stores ran low on fresh produce.
The following is a breakdown of affected sectors.
PETROL/FUEL - Truckers on Tuesday sealed off a petrol depot at Grigny which supplies 90 percent of petrol sold in hypermarkets in the Paris region.
The Oil Industry Association said half the nation's 175 fuel depots were blocked. Heating fuel was getting through, but 500 out of 18,000 petrol stations were dry, up from 100 on Monday.
Shell's largest French refinery, in Rouen, a Total refinery at Notre-Dame-de-Gravenchon, and the Grandpuits refinery in Seine-et-Marne were sealed off by truckers.
In Normandy, all petrol depots and refineries near Rouen were cut off. In certain regions including the Pas-de-Calais, officials are rationing petrol supplies to private car owners.
Local authorities in many areas ordered petrol stations to supply only firemen, ambulances and other emergency services, or ration sales to private motorists.
GRAIN - The strike is disrupting grain supplies to French ports, officials said. "Most access roads are blocked, but the main concern is petrol shortages," one official said.
In the northern port of Dunkirk, silo officials said trucks could still use the Paris-Lille highway to supply silos.
Another official said inventories were low, and that if the strike lasted one more week, ship loadings could be disrupted.

In the southwestern port of Bordeaux officials at the SIGMA silo said the strike was curtailing grain supplies activity. But because silos are full of newly harvested maize, ship loadings are proceeding at the normal pace, he said.
AGRO-FOOD - The sector is temporarily shedding workers and could run up big losses if the strike goes on, industry officials said on Tuesday.
"If the situation were to last two or three more days, we could all be on temporary leave," said Philippe Cousseau, head of logistics for the National Agro-Food Industry Association.
He said producers of dairy products, poultry, ready-made meals, fruits and vegetables were among the hardest hit by the crisis, which could result in "very heavy" financial losses.

Around 20 animal feed plants have temporary laid off staff and 100 more, out of a total of 380, may be affected by Wednesday, said Paul Hervieu, spokesman of the National Animal Feed Makers Association. He warned that if the strike went on longer, farmers would have trouble feeding pigs and chickens.
RETAIL - Supermarkets in the truck-besieged towns of Caen, Bordeaux and Avignon were the hardest hit by the strike.
"We got the feeling this morning that the strike movement is getting tougher, particularly in the North where the Vendin warehouse is cut off," said a Promodes spokesman.

CARGO - Air France Cargo said the situation would become critical if the strike continued. "The situation has become difficult, with services running behind schedule. However, we have not yet reached crisis point which could be the case if the dispute were prolonged," an airline official said.
The airline's trucking services are hardest hit around Bordeaux, the Spanish and German borders, and the port towns of Calais and Dover, the official said.

CARS - The truckers' strike has disrupted production at several car plants unable to obtain parts but the impact is muted because production slowdowns had been scheduled as a result of weak demand for cars.
